caption: Figure. Urinary tract infection by level. Most infections ascend from the urethra; fever, flank pain and white blood cell casts place the infection in the kidney.

Figure. Where immune deposits sit in the glomerular capillary wall: subendothelial and mesangial deposits drive nephritic inflammation, subepithelial deposits mainly injure podocytes, linear IgG marks anti-GBM disease, and pauci-immune GN has none.
Figure. Nephritic versus nephrotic: the dominant injury (inflammation versus podocyte damage) predicts the urine, the blood pressure and the complications.
Figure. Renal cystic disease at a glance: cyst pattern and kidney size separate simple and complex cysts, ADPKD, ARPKD, acquired cystic disease and medullary sponge kidney.

Figure. Urinary tract tumours by cell of origin: clear cell and papillary carcinoma from the proximal tubule, oncocytoma and chromophobe carcinoma from intercalated cells, urothelial carcinoma from the lining of the pelvis, ureter and bladder, and Wilms tumour from metanephric blastema.
Figure. Urine casts and what each points to. Casts are moulded in tubules, so their contents come from the kidney.
Figure. Nephron segments, their main transporters and the diuretic that acts on each (red). Original Naadi diagram.
Figure. Renal tubular acidosis types 1, 2 and 4 compared: defect, serum potassium, urine pH, stones and classic causes. Original Naadi diagram.
Figure. Unilateral renal artery stenosis. The stenotic kidney releases renin and depends on angiotensin II constriction of the efferent arteriole; the contralateral kidney suppresses its renin.

Figure. Neurogenic bladder by level of lesion: above the pons, the bladder is overactive but coordinated; in the spinal cord above the sacral segments, overactive with detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia; at or below the sacral cord, underactive with retention.
Figure. Kidney development: the ureteric bud forms the collecting system and the metanephric mesenchyme forms the nephron; a horseshoe kidney stops ascending under the inferior mesenteric artery.
Figure. Where common nephrotoxic drugs act along the nephron, from the glomerular arterioles to the bladder.
Figure. Glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in the beta cell and where glucose-lowering drugs act.
Figure. Schematic time-action profiles of insulin preparations after subcutaneous injection.
Figure. Hypoglycemia: the laboratory pattern of each cause, using blood drawn while glucose is low. C-peptide marks the body's own insulin; low ketones mean insulin or IGF-2 is acting.
Figure. Thyroid hormone synthesis in the follicular cell (trapping, organification, coupling, release) and the step each drug blocks.
Figure. Reading TSH together with free T4. Primary disease moves TSH opposite to free T4; pituitary disease does not.
Figure. Calcium, phosphate and PTH patterns that separate the main disorders of calcium metabolism.
Figure. Work-up of an adrenal incidentaloma: test every mass for hormone excess and judge cancer risk from size and CT attenuation.
Figure. Hypothalamic-pituitary axes and their feedback loops. The posterior pituitary stores ADH and oxytocin made in hypothalamic nuclei.
Figure. Reading a water deprivation test: urine osmolality after deprivation and after desmopressin in primary polydipsia, central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (illustrative values).
Figure. Hypothalamic nuclei, their normal roles and the effect of a lesion in each.
Figure. Multiple endocrine neoplasia: MEN1 is loss of the menin tumour suppressor; MEN2A and MEN2B are activating RET variants affecting neural crest-derived C cells and chromaffin cells.

Figure. Adrenal steroid synthesis. The 21-hydroxylase block lowers cortisol and aldosterone and diverts precursors to androgens; 11β- and 17α-hydroxylase blocks raise 11-deoxycorticosterone and blood pressure.
Figure. Exogenous glucocorticoids suppress CRH and ACTH; the adrenal cortex atrophies, so abrupt withdrawal causes secondary adrenal insufficiency with preserved aldosterone.
